summary: Year 2 children (ages 6-7) write simple fractions of quantities (e.g. 1/2 of 6 = 3) and meet their first fraction equivalence: 2/4 = 1/2. Equivalence means two differently-written fractions name the same amount - the same-sized piece, cut into a different number of parts. This is the natural place to confront the whole-number bias that '2/4 must be more than 1/2 because the numbers are bigger'. The core teaching move is predict-then-check: the child predicts a comparison, then overlays two quarters onto one half to see them coincide exactly.
misconceptions: 2/4 is more than 1/2 because the numbers are bigger (whole-number bias)
Two fractions written with different numbers cannot name the same amount (no concept of equivalence)
Errors computing a unit fraction of a quantity (1/2 of 6) by not sharing equally

activities.title: Overlay check: proving 1/2 = 2/4 by covering
steps: Take two identical chocolate bars (or paper strips of the same length). Cut one into 2 equal pieces and the other into 4 equal pieces.
Before moving anything, predict and say aloud: are 2 pieces from the four-piece bar MORE, LESS, or the SAME as 1 piece from the two-piece bar? Give your reason.
Place the two quarter-pieces exactly on top of the one half-piece and check whether they cover it with nothing left over and no overlap.
Write the result as a fraction sentence: 1/2 = 2/4, and say in words 'the same amount, cut into a different number of parts'.
Find at least one more name for the same amount (for example cut another identical bar into 6 and check that 3/6 also covers one half).
activities.insight: Two quarters cover exactly one half, so 2/4 and 1/2 name the same amount even though 2/4 uses bigger numbers. A fraction has many names for one value. The prediction step surfaces the 'bigger numbers = more' intuition so the overlay can confront it directly.

activities.title: Equal sharing: deriving equivalent fractions
steps: Share 4 pizzas equally among 8 children by drawing or using counters; work out how much each child gets.
Write the share each child receives as a fraction (4/8), then show by grouping that this is also 2/4 and 1/2.
Explain in your own words why 4/8, 2/4 and 1/2 all describe the same share.
activities.insight: Equivalent fractions arise naturally from equal sharing: the same real share can be written with different numbers, and these names are equal.

activities.title: Finding a fraction of a quantity by equal sharing
steps: Take a set of 6 counters. Share them into 2 equal groups and count one group to find 1/2 of 6.
Write the sentence 1/2 of 6 = 3 next to your groups.
Try 1/2 of 10 by sharing 10 into 2 equal groups, and write 1/2 of 10 = 5.

Now find 2/4 of 6. Sharing 6 counters into 4 equal groups does not give whole counters (each group would be one and a half), so use the equivalence 2/4 = 1/2: since 1/2 of 6 = 3, we know 2/4 of 6 is also 3.
activities.insight: A unit fraction of a quantity is found by sharing equally into the number of parts named by the denominator and taking one group. Because 2/4 = 1/2, taking 2/4 of a quantity gives the same result as taking 1/2 of it.

activities.title: Many names on one point: number line and matching
steps: Mark 0 and 1 at the ends of a strip or line. Fold or measure to place 1/2, then divide the same line into quarters and place 2/4.
Check that 1/2 and 2/4 land on exactly the same point.
Match written fractions to their equal partners (for example pair 1/2 with 2/4), explaining why each pair is equal and why a 'bigger numbers' pairing would be wrong.
Say or write a short justification: 'They are at the same point, so they are the same amount.'
activities.insight: Equivalent fractions occupy the same position on the number line, giving another way to see that different names can mean one value. Matching tasks let the child rehearse recognising equivalent pairs and rejecting 'bigger-number' traps.

checkQuestion: Show two identical chocolate bars. One is cut into 2 equal pieces and you take 1 piece; the other is cut into 4 equal pieces and you take 2 pieces. Ask: 'Do you have the same amount of chocolate, more, or less? How do you know?' Then ask: 'So what can you say about the fractions 1/2 and 2/4?'
checkAnswer: The same amount. 1/2 and 2/4 are equivalent - they name the same-sized piece, just cut into a different number of parts. Two quarters cover exactly one half. (Tier 2: 1/2 = 2/4.)
